title: The Odyssey
subtitle: The Long Way Home
attribution: An original abridged adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey
description: A familiar dog, an old scar and a bow lead a stranger into his own hall.
intro: The house remembers him before its guests do.
ending: The hall was his again. Recognition was still another matter.
stageLabel: A pixel art retelling of the Odyssey

adaptationSource.title: Homer, Odyssey, Books XVII–XXII
adaptationSource.note: Original abridged English narration and dialogue. Events are condensed for quiet episodic reading. Ritual sacrifice and deaths are represented without gore. The final conflict of Book XXIV is condensed to Athena intervening before renewed bloodshed.

steps.text: Telemachus had gone ahead to the house. Eumaeus led Odysseus out along the path, carrying their secret.

steps.text: Telemachus was already at the palace. The next morning, Odysseus followed him, wearing Athena’s disguise and walking with Eumaeus.
On the path to his house, Odysseus found Argos, the dog he had raised before leaving for Troy.
The old hound lifted his head. Disguise meant nothing to him. His master was here.
“He was quick once. No one could outrun him.”
Odysseus turned aside to hide a tear. He could not kneel and greet the dog without giving himself away.
Argos closed his eyes. After twenty years of waiting, he died knowing that his master had returned.
For the first time, someone at home had recognized him. The gate still waited ahead.

steps.text: Telemachus kept their secret. He was elsewhere in the house, waiting for the right moment to help his father.
Later that evening, after Eumaeus brought him into the palace, Penelope questioned the old traveler beside the fire.
“Many travelers have brought me stories. Some only wanted a meal.”
“Then ask me something a story cannot easily borrow.”
He described the cloak Odysseus had worn, and its clasp. She listened more closely, but still held back.
“I remember fastening it.”
She spoke of the years she had kept the suitors waiting. He heard the cost of the time he had called a journey.
She asked Eurycleia to wash the traveler’s feet. Kindness, too, could uncover a secret.
Eurycleia brought the basin to his bare foot. As she washed his leg, her hand found the old scar.
A boar had wounded him as a boy. She had known that mark long before he became a king.
“Odysseus.”
“Not yet. Keep this between us.”
She steadied the basin. Penelope had not seen what her hands had found.
The old nurse knew. His son knew. Each small recognition made the stranger harder to keep hidden.
Penelope planned a test for the next day. The suitors would have to use the great bow that Odysseus had left at home.

steps.text: The next morning, Penelope offered the suitors a challenge: string Odysseus’s bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe openings.
She would marry the man who passed the test. The bow was difficult to bend, and none of the suitors could string it.
Antinous was one of the suitors. He was still treating the palace as his own, without knowing who the old traveler was.
Antinous took it. He pulled at the wood, but could not bend it far enough to set the string.
“Let the old traveler try.”
The suitors protested. Telemachus insisted, and asked his mother to return to her chamber.
Odysseus took the bow in his hands. He checked it as carefully as if the years might have damaged it.
He strung it without strain. The cord gave one clear note. Telemachus moved to his father’s side.
The arrow passed through all twelve axes. The hall was still before anyone understood why.
Father and son had planned this together. Earlier, Telemachus had put the suitors’ weapons away where they could not reach them.
Eumaeus secured the doors as they had planned. Telemachus turned back toward his father, who still held the bow.
“You thought I would never return.”
He turned the bow on Antinous. The feast was over. No one in the hall still thought he was a beggar.
The first arrow killed Antinous. Then, with his son and loyal servants beside him, Odysseus killed the other suitors. Those who had taken no part were spared.
When it was over, he stopped the servants from celebrating over the dead. The house would have to live with this morning.
The hall belonged to him again. Upstairs, Penelope still needed to know who had truly come home.
